title: Health Care Systems Around the World
summary: Final installment of a four-part healthcare reform series. Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant, with guest Dr. Molly Edmonds, take a "hot air balloon ride" tour of health care systems around the world: France (ranked number one by the WHO in 2000, mixed public and supplemental insurance), Germany (sickness funds dating to Bismarck and guilds, frequent reforms, disease management programs, doctor pay concerns), Cuba (preventive care, home doctor visits, two-tier system and statistics questions, medical exports), China (dismantled cooperative system, rural divide, planned clinic building and funding questions), Taiwan (smart card with medical history, low costs, rising premiums), Russia (underfunded public-private system, informal bribes, low spending), Canada (single-payer with private hospitals, wait times, cheaper drugs and surgery), and Switzerland (expensive, mandatory private insurance with subsidies, nonprofit insurers). Dr. Michael Roizen of the Cleveland Clinic is quoted on competitiveness. The episode closes with thanks and listener contact information.

segments.title: Opening and framing the healthcare reform series
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the final installment of the healthcare reform series with guest Dr. Molly Edmonds. They recap the uninsured, US chronic disease and mortality rates, and the idea that the system hurts US global competitiveness. Dr. Michael Roizen is quoted on reform and competitiveness with Europe and Asia.

segments.title: France health care system
segments.summary: Molly describes France as rated number one by the WHO in 2000. Citizens pay income-based contributions, the government covers about 70 percent, and supplemental public or private insurance covers the rest. Critics say it is divided by class, and there is weak coordination between GPs and specialists. France has a low rate of preventable deaths.
topics: World Health Organization health system rankings

segments.title: Germany health insurance system
segments.summary: Germany's system of employer and employee funded sickness insurance plans traces back to Otto von Bismarck and medieval guilds. The system is reformed often. Disease management programs with nurse counseling lower hospitalization and death rates. German doctors reportedly earn about two-thirds of US doctors' pay but pay less for malpractice insurance. Higher earners can opt for regulated private insurance.

segments.title: Cuba health care and preventive care
segments.summary: Cuba is discussed for its preventive care, including yearly doctor home visits. Michael Moore's film is mentioned, and critics claim a two-tier system with health tourism. Hosts raise questions about how Cuba's statistics are counted, including infant mortality and abortion concerns. Cuba's medical and pharmaceutical exports, including meningitis B and hepatitis B vaccines, are also noted.

segments.title: China rural healthcare reform
segments.summary: China dismantled its cooperative healthcare system, which created a large divide between urban and rural care. A proposal for farmers to pay a dollar a year was seen as too expensive. China plans to build clinics in rural areas, and funding from central and provincial governments is uncertain.

segments.title: Taiwan smart card health system
segments.summary: Taiwan's system uses a smart card holding a patient's full medical history, which lowers administrative costs. Taiwan's spending no longer covers costs, and premiums are rising. An average family premium is cited as about 650 dollars a year.

segments.title: Russia health care system
segments.summary: Russia dismantled its Soviet system for a public-private mix that works poorly in practice. The government does not pay enough, so patients are pressured for informal payments. Russia spends about three percent of its spending on healthcare against the WHO's recommended five percent. Foreign Policy ranked Russia among the four worst systems, and the US also appeared on that list.

segments.title: Canada single-payer system and wait times
segments.summary: Canada's single-payer system is often compared to the US, though hospitals and doctors are private. Taxes fund the system and money flows to provinces. Wait times are mainly for elective surgeries and have improved since the 1990s investment. Open heart surgery is cheaper in Toronto than Chicago, and drugs are cheaper in Canada.

segments.title: Switzerland health insurance and wrap-up
segments.summary: Switzerland has expensive, mandatory private health plans that are not tied to employment. Subsidies help people who cannot afford them. Premiums are the same for everyone regardless of income. The hosts close the series, thank Dr. Roizen and Molly, and invite listener questions by email.
